approvedAsIs.name: Giant Puffball
reasons: File and entry: /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/foraging-research/corrected-pass1.json, index 10 of 18, name "Giant Puffball" (single occurrence, no duplicate).

No deadly lookalike is missing. The one that kills people here — the button/'egg' stage of deadly Amanita (A. bisporigera / A. virosa group, A. phalloides) — is present, listed as "deadly", and the tell is the correct universal test: a vertical slice top-to-bottom through the middle showing cap silhouette, developing gill arc, central stem and membranous veil, versus uniform marshmallow-white. Critically, it instructs slicing EVERY ball with no size exemption and explicitly states "size is never a clearance" — the single most common way this ID protocol gets fatally shortcut. It adds a second independent check at the base (sac-like volva vs. one thick white mycelial cord) and tells the forager to cut at ground level and look rather than snip blind.

The other two confusion classes are covered and correctly graded: Scleroderma earthballs as "toxic" (correct — GI toxin, not fatal) and stinkhorn eggs as "unpalatable". The Scleroderma tell is unusually good adversarially: it refuses to lean on interior colour alone or on the 'small and yellow-warted' stereotype, and explicitly flags S. polyrhizum as whitish, smooth, 8-13 cm and growing in lawns and disturbed urban ground — i.e. the same ground, same size class, same colour as the target. Rind-vs-no-rind, reddish blush on the cut, rubbery vs. spongy are all real, checkable, and available on the exact material being harvested.

The tells work on the part and season actually harvested. There is only one part (the whole fruitbody) and one life stage (immature, all-white), and every tell is a cross-section or base check performed on that fruitbody in the field. Nothing depends on a flower, a mature stage, or a feature absent at harvest time.
caution "expert" is correct and required — a deadly lookalike exists.

Schema conformance is clean: all required keys present, no extra keys; caution and all three lookalikes[].danger values are legal; regions (northeast, midwest, southeast) and terrain (meadow, edge, disturbed, woodland) are all valid ids; months [6,7,8,9,10] are legal 0-indexed values.

Months are correctly 0-indexed and match the prose: July-November, with the habitat text independently saying Sept-Oct peak (~80% of records), August good in the north, July flushes after heavy rain, and "a few lingering into November". The November tail confirms 0-indexing rather than an off-by-one 1-indexed array. The entry also correctly declines to follow MDC's May-October Missouri range, noting spring finds are rare.

Required safety preparation is present and specific where specificity matters: peel the tough outer skin, discard the WHOLE puffball at the first sign of yellow/olive/brown/powdery interior rather than trimming back to white, do not wash, avoid sprayed lawns/verges/dog-walked parks, and eat only a small portion the first time. The lycoperdonosis warning (don't crush mature ones or breathe the dust; CDC MMWR Wisconsin 1994, eight adolescents hospitalised) is a genuine hazard most guides omit.

MINOR, not blocking — "cook thoroughly" is the only prep verb; unlike the sibling Lion's Mane and Chicken of the Woods entries, this one never states "never eat it raw" outright. There is no established minimum cooking time for Calvatia gigantea (no timed toxin like the morel's), so no duration is missing, but I'd add the explicit no-raw sentence for house-style consistency and because raw puffball does cause GI upset in some people.

MINOR, not blocking — terrain includes "woodland" while the habitat sentence opens "Open ground rather than deep woods". Since terrain is the primary grouping axis, this surfaces the entry under "Woodland floor", which is where the deadly Amanitas actually live. The ID protocol (slice everything, regardless) neutralises the risk, but dropping "woodland" and keeping edge/meadow/disturbed would match the entry's own text.

MINOR, not blocking — region tension the entry itself discloses: "southeast" is listed although the habitat text says records thin south of the Appalachians and the species is effectively absent from Florida and the Gulf, where C. craniiformis is the common big white puffball. It is defensible for TN/KY/NC, and the habitat text warns the reader, so it does not send anyone to the wrong place unwarned. Conversely "southcentral" (TX/OK) is omitted despite the cited "Great Plains eastward" distribution — an under-report, which is the safe direction to err.

Sourcing supports the safety-critical claims independently of any single source: MDC, NPS (the cross-section test), NC State (volva, amatoxin timeline), Kuo/MushroomExpert (range, C. booniana separation, S. polyrhizum morphology), Cornell, CDC MMWR. The March 2026 Humboldt County news item is a supporting anecdote only — no safety instruction rests on it.

approvedAsIs.name: Morel
reasons: Deadly-lookalike coverage is complete. Gyromitra (false morels/lorchels) is present at danger 'deadly', covering both the eastern species (G. caroliniana, G. brunnea) and the western G. esculenta group (G. splendida, G. venenata). No other genuinely deadly morel confuser exists — Verpa and Helvella are the remaining real ones and both are listed at 'toxic'. Nothing deadly is missing.

The Gyromitra tell is layered correctly and works on the exact part and season harvested (the whole fresh spring fruitbody): primary test is cap morphology (irregular brainlike lobes bulging OUTWARD vs a honeycomb of pits pressed inward), confirmed by the lengthwise slice (true morel hollow cap-tip to stem-base; Gyromitra chambered, cottony, or solid). Critically, it refuses to let habitat act as a filter — it states outright that Gyromitra is abundant in montane conifer forest, favours burned ground, and fruits at snowmelt, i.e. the same burn sites and the same fortnight as western burn morels. It also refuses the whole genus including the low-gyromitrin snowbank species (G. montana, G. korfii), which is the right call since they cannot be sorted from lethal relatives by eye.

The Verpa tell is unusually well constructed. It leads with cap attachment (free except at the apex) rather than the stem-pith test, and explicitly warns that the pith test fails — older Verpa lose the pith and a hollow Verpa would pass a naive slice test. It then pre-empts the opposite error by naming half-free morels (Morchella punctipes east, M. populiphila west) as legitimate true morels attached about halfway down: 'attached halfway is fine; attached only at the tip is not.' That is the single most common beginner trap in this genus and it is handled.
caution: 'expert' is correct — a deadly lookalike (Gyromitra) exists.

Required safety preparation is present and specific, not vague. Never raw; slice each one lengthwise (identification step and de-bugging); rinse; cook thoroughly with a stated duration ('ten minutes or more of real heat'); never with alcohol; small portion the first time; do not eat in quantity; discard anything soft, dark or waterlogged. The 2023 Montana outbreak (51 ill, 3 hospitalised, 2 dead, correctly identified species from a clean commercial source, served under-cooked) is cited to make 'cooking is not optional' concrete. This is the one entry-level mistake that kills people with correctly identified morels, and it is covered.

Months are right. [1,2,3,4,5,6] is 0-indexed Feb–Jul, matching the stated wave: Deep South from late February through early April, Midwest/Northeast peaking late April into May, high-elevation Cascade burn morels June into July (Cascades fall in 'west', so month 6 is justified for a listed region).

Schema is clean: all required fields present, no extra keys, caution/danger/terrain/region values all valid enum members, months integers in 0–11, 13 sources with URLs to state agencies (Michigan DNR, Missouri Conservation), CDC MMWR, FDA and primary literature.

NON-BLOCKING BUT SHOULD BE FIXED BEFORE PUBLISH — regions omits 'mountain' (MT, WY, CO, NM, AZ, UT, ID, NV) while the habitat prose explicitly describes 'high-elevation Rocky Mountain and Cascade burn morels' and 'the West, Southwest and Northwest'. forageFor() in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/foraging.ts filters on regions, so a Colorado, Montana, Idaho or Utah forager sees no morel entry at all — the Rockies burn-morel forager, who is the single most Gyromitra-exposed audience and who lives in the state of the outbreak this entry itself cites. I am not blocking on it because the failure mode is withholding, not misleading: nobody eats the wrong thing because an entry is absent, and any reader who does reach the entry gets the correct habitat prose. 'southcentral' (TX, OK) is a smaller gap of the same kind — Oklahoma has a real morel season. Note the same four-region set is used for every mushroom in this file, so this may be a house convention rather than a Morel-specific slip.

COSMETIC — terrain includes 'upland' (dry rocky slopes, barrens). Defensible for western conifer burn slopes, but odd for a mushroom whose classic ground is hardwood bottomland and floodplain; it places Morel under 'Dry slopes & barrens' in the terrain walk. woodland/edge/wetland/disturbed already carry it, so nothing is lost.

COSMETIC — the single months array is shared across all listed regions, so a Southeast user sees Morel in June–July although the entry's own prose ends the Deep South season in early April. This is structural to the schema (every entry behaves this way) and the habitat text states the regional timing explicitly, so it cannot send anyone to a wrong identification.

COSMETIC — the citation gloss 'Michigan DNR describes the beefsteak morel by its solid stem' compresses that source slightly (its emphasis is on the cottony/chambered interior). The practical instruction the reader acts on — it must be hollow the whole way or you refuse it — is correct either way.

approvedAsIs.name: Oyster Mushroom
reasons: Both deadly lookalikes that matter for a shelf-shaped wood mushroom are present and correctly ranked: angel wings (Pleurocybella porrigens, 'deadly') and deadly galerina (Galerina marginata, 'deadly'). Jack-o'-lantern is correctly 'toxic' (violent GI, not fatal) with the decisive cut-in-half orange-flesh test, and Crepidotus / Lentinellus ursinus are correctly 'unpalatable'. No missing deadly confusable found: sulphur tuft and Sarcomyxa/Phyllotopsis are either less confusable than Galerina (already covered by the central-stem + ring + rusty-print tell) or not dangerous, and the flat rule 'on wood only, never rising from soil' rules out the soil-dwelling deadly genera (Amanita, Entoloma, Clitocybe) up front.

The angel wings tell is the strongest part of the entry and is written the conservative way round: it judges the flesh (paper-thin, floppy, translucent, chalky white, no stem, 2-10 cm) rather than the substrate, and explicitly states that 'it was on a hardwood log' does NOT clear a thin white shelf, citing Burke Herbarium for P. pulmonarius on PNW conifer wood. That closes the exact failure mode that gets people hurt here. The 2004 Japan outbreak figures (59 sickened, 17 dead, acute encephalopathy, victims with chronic kidney disease, toxin still unidentified) are accurate, and it correctly concludes the species is unsafe for anyone rather than 'safe if your kidneys are fine'.

caution 'expert' is correct per the type contract (deadly lookalike exists), and schema validation is clean: all 12 months are valid 0-indexed ints; regions are all valid RegionIds; terrain values are all valid; every lookalike has name/danger/tell with danger in the allowed union; all required ForageSpecies fields are present; 12 sources, all extension services, state agencies, herbaria or MushroomExpert.

Season handling is right rather than lazily broad. months 0-11 looks alarming until you read the habitat field, which explains the three-species calendar split (P. ostreatus roughly Oct-Apr including post-thaw mild spells, P. pulmonarius late Apr-Sep, P. populinus on aspen/cottonwood in early summer) and warns that deep-winter northern finds only happen during thaws. That matches Kuo. Because Galerina is also year-round and is listed, no month surfaces this entry without its deadly warning attached.

NON-BLOCKING FIX 1 (regions): 'mountain' and 'southcentral' are omitted, which contradicts the entry's own text. P. populinus is called out as an aspen/cottonwood species and aspen's American stronghold is the Rockies (CO/UT/WY/MT/NM), and oysters are common in TX/OK. This is under-inclusion, so it hides the entry from those foragers rather than sending anyone to the wrong place - not a safety inversion, but it should be corrected to include mountain and southcentral.

NON-BLOCKING FIX 2 (Galerina gill wording): the tell says Galerina's 'gills stop where they meet the stem rather than running down it'. Kuo and NC State Extension both describe G. marginata gills as attached to SLIGHTLY DECURRENT. A galerina with faintly running gills could be read as passing the oyster test on that one sub-tell. It is not decisive here because the same tell also gives the central stem, the ring/ring-zone, the tawny sticky cap and the rusty-brown print, and instructs a spore print on any doubt - but the wording should be softened to 'attached to at most slightly decurrent, never running onto a lateral stub'.

NON-BLOCKING FIX 3 (taste test): the Lentinellus ursinus tell instructs 'a tiny nibble, spat out'. Chew-and-spit is standard mycological practice and here it is a confirmatory step on an already brown, hairy, saw-toothed-gilled mushroom - neither angel wings (smooth, pure white) nor Galerina (stemmed, ringed) fits that description at the point the nibble is reached. Still, in an 'expert' entry it should carry an explicit qualifier: only after the deadly lookalikes are ruled out, and never swallow.

NON-BLOCKING FIX 4 (preparation specificity): 'always cooked through' plus 'never eat them raw - raw oysters cause gastrointestinal upset' plus 'eat a small portion the first time' is the correct set of warnings, and unlike fiddleheads or acorns there is no established critical detox duration for Pleurotus, so no required preparation step is missing. It would still read better as a concrete instruction, e.g. sauté until the released liquid has cooked off, roughly 8-10 minutes.

MINOR/COSMETIC: terrain includes 'upland' (dry rocky slopes, barrens, pine and oak scrub), which is a stretch for a fungus that needs moist dead wood - dropping it would be more honest, though it creates no hazard since the entry already refuses to let conifer or hardwood substrate clear a thin white shelf. The harvest field is good practice throughout: cut rather than tear, pass on slimy or sour-smelling clusters, leave pins and the largest spore-shedders, and avoid road shoulders, creosote ties and treated lumber because Pleurotus is a strong bioaccumulator used for mycoremediation.

approvedAsIs.name: Golden Chanterelle
reasons: No deadly lookalike is missing. The two that most chanterelle write-ups omit are both here and both graded 'deadly': the orellanine webcaps (Cortinarius rubellus/orellanus/orellanosus/armillatus, with the 3-to-20-day delayed renal failure and the fact that cooking/drying/freezing don't destroy the toxin) and Paxillus involutus (delayed immune haemolytic anaemia, plus the crucial point that prior uneventful meals give no protection). Jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus illudens/subilludens/olivascens), Gymnopilus, Hygrophoropsis and Turbinellus floccosus round out the list and cover East, Gulf, Midwest and West Coast fruiting.

Danger grades are right: 'expert' caution matches two genuinely deadly lookalikes; jack-o'-lantern is correctly 'toxic' rather than 'deadly' (severe illudin-S GI, rarely fatal in a healthy adult) with the dehydration risk to children and the elderly called out.

The tells are all season- and part-independent, which is what matters for a mushroom: true blade-like separable gills vs blunt forking false ridges continuous with the flesh, spore print colour (pale cream vs rust-brown vs clay-brown), flesh colour on a slice (white/pale and string-cheese fibrous vs orange through cap and stem), Paxillus's reddish-brown bruising, and Omphalotus's fusion at a common base. Every one of these is checkable on the exact thing that goes in the basket, at any time of year.

It actively defeats the two heuristics that get beginners poisoned: 'it grew out of the ground' (habitat explicitly says jack-o'-lanterns erupt from buried roots and look terrestrial, and that both deadly lookalikes are soil fungi in the same woods) and 'it doesn't glow' (glow needs total darkness and dark-adapted eyes, fades with age, absence proves nothing). The C. lateritius caveat also fails safe: if you can't resolve forking ridges, leave it.
Schema-valid: all 12 fields present, caution/danger/terrain values in-enum, months are legal 0-indexed integers, regions are valid RegionIds, sources are real extension/USFS/NAMA citations.

NON-BLOCKING FIX: regions omits 'mountain' while the habitat text explicitly describes the Southwest sky islands and Mogollon Rim (AZ/NM = the 'mountain' region per src/data/seasonal-regional.ts) fruiting July–September in the monsoon. That is an internal contradiction and it hides the entry — and its deadly-lookalike warnings — from Arizona and New Mexico users. It under-includes rather than misdirects, so it isn't a hazard, but 'mountain' should be added, and 'southcentral' is worth considering for east Texas and Oklahoma oak woods.

NON-BLOCKING: months is a union across regions, so Jan/Feb (from coastal California C. californicus) and Nov/Dec (from the Northwest) surface for Northeast/Midwest/Southeast users when nothing is fruiting there. The schema has no per-region months and other entries do the same; the habitat field spells the per-region seasons out precisely, and no one identifies a mushroom by the calendar, so this is a wasted walk rather than a risk.

NON-BLOCKING WORDING: 'Take a SPORE PRINT ... this one test settles it' is scoped to the webcap bullet, where it is true, but a beginner could over-generalize it — a spore print does NOT separate a jack-o'-lantern (pale) from a chanterelle. Suggest 'settles webcaps' or similar.

NON-BLOCKING: the prep instruction ('always cooked, never raw', dry-sauté then finish with fat, small first portion, keep an uncooked specimen for ID) covers what this species actually requires — unlike morels there is no specific documented minimum time — but adding 'cook thoroughly, several minutes, never taste raw to test' would tighten it.

NON-BLOCKING NITS: 'upland' terrain is a stretch for a moisture-dependent mycorrhizal fungus, though eastern well-drained oak slopes justify it; and Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca at 'unpalatable' is defensible but 'toxic' would be more conservative given the reported GI upset the tell itself mentions.

approvedAsIs.name: Lion's Mane (Bearded Tooth)
reasons: No deadly lookalike is missing. There is no deadly white, unbranched, spine-bearing fungus on North American hardwood; the genus Hericium contains no toxic species. The entry names all three benign confusables (H. coralloides, H. americanum, Hydnum repandum) plus H. abietis for conifer finds in the West, and correctly states a mix-up among them is not dangerous. Hydnoid terrestrial genera (Sarcodon, Hydnellum) and gilled toxins (Amanita, Galerina) share no character with a single white icicle cushion on a trunk wound.
caution 'care' is correctly calibrated: 'expert' would be wrong since no deadly lookalike exists, and 'easy' would understate the two tough polypore mimics and the documented idiosyncratic reaction.

Both lookalike tells work on the part actually harvested (the whole fresh fruiting body) and in the season actually harvested. Climacodon septentrionalis is separated by stacked overlapping shelves with teeth only on each underside vs. a single attachment point with long soft spines over the whole surface; Irpiciporus pachyodon by blunt flattened teeth mixed with angular pores on a resupinate crust vs. round-section soft spines and no pores anywhere.

Both tells explicitly disqualify the unreliable shortcuts rather than relying on them: 'Do not use the host tree to rule it out' for Climacodon (same hosts, same late-summer-to-autumn window) and 'Same hosts (oaks) and same season, so judge by the underside, not the tree' for Irpiciporus. This is the correct handling of a genuine host and season overlap.

Safety preparation is present and specific, not vague: always cook, never eat raw; reject any specimen that has yellowed or softened as sour and often bacterially spoiled; and a concrete first-time protocol of a small portion with a one-day wait for the minority idiosyncratic reaction, sourced to Missouri Dept. of Conservation.

Months [7,8,9,10,11,0] = Aug-Jan are correct and the habitat text resolves them regionally: Sept-Nov in the East and Midwest, Nov-Jan on the West Coast. August is marginally early for the East but sends nobody anywhere hazardous.

Regions (midwest, northeast, southeast, west) are each backed by a cited source: MDC and Minnesota DNR for midwest, UF/IFAS Escambia County for southeast, MykoWeb California and the GBIF voucher facet for west. The habitat correctly notes there is no native beech west of the Great Plains and gives the western hosts (live oak, Oregon white oak, bigleaf maple) instead.

Schema conforms exactly: all twelve fields present, caution in the union, both lookalike danger values 'unpalatable' in the union, months 0-indexed integers in 0-11, terrain ['woodland','edge'] and all four region ids valid per RegionId in src/data/seasonal-regional.ts.

Non-blocking note: 'southcentral' is omitted though H. erinaceus reaches the oak-hickory forests of eastern Texas and Oklahoma. This is under-inclusive rather than misleading, errs on the safe side, and matches the file's stated policy of leaving out what the cited sources do not cover.

Non-blocking note: 'a hericium on a conifer in the West is H. abietis' is slightly loose, since H. coralloides also fruits on conifers. Both are edible, so the imprecision carries no safety consequence.

Non-blocking note: the harvest guidance is sound conservation practice (cut at the attachment point, leave the bark and base so the wound refruits, take only white specimens, leave some fruitings) and the entry makes no medicinal claims.
